//: Floors for the markup oracles, held from BOTH sides: dropping below one is a regression, and rising above one is an improvement that has to be recorded here in the same commit that earns it. Data rather than code, because these numbers move as the library grows and the diff is the point.
//loop: markup -> tree -> shrubbery -> tree -> markup equals markup -> tree -> markup. The headline property. Both sides are first normalised for the three things the notation cannot say -- an implied end tag, a void element's slash, a character reference's spelling -- so a file that does NOT close is a bug rather than a design limit. That is why every bucket is at 100%, including the deliberately broken one: a recovery that survives the detour is a real claim.
//roundtrip: Printing is a fixed point: print, reparse, print, compare, in pretty and minified. Expected to stay at 100%: a printer that is not idempotent grows the file every time it is run, which is worse than one that is merely ugly.
//conform: Our printed output, parsed by `moonbit-community/html`, builds the same document the input does. The only oracle here with an external reference, and the only property a formatter actually owes anyone: it does not require our tree to be a document tree -- it deliberately is not -- it requires our tree to be document-EQUIVALENT. Printed with `whitespace=Strict`, because the default policy is ALLOWED to drop whitespace between block children and measuring the tree and the policy in one number would mean neither could be read.
//conform-gap:
Five files do not conform, and each is named because a floor below 100% must not silently absorb somebody's bug. TWO ARE OURS, by design: `adoption.html` needs the adoption agency and `end-tag-void.html` needs `
` to become a `
`, and both invent or move nodes, which is exactly what a markup tree is defined not to do. THREE ARE THE REFERENCE'S, checked against Chromium's DOMParser rather than asserted: it reads `` as a node HTML does not have, where the specification says bogus comment (`processing-instruction.html`, and `rhombus-xml...xml.shrub` in the notation corpus); and it does not apply generic RCDATA parsing to a `` in body, so `<div><title>a<b>c</b>` gives it element children where Chromium and this library both give it text (`rhombus-html-lib...parser.shrub`). If a later version of the reference fixes either, the floor rises and the ratchet will say so.
//tokens: The html5lib tokenizer suite, vendored under test/html/corpus/html5lib and counted per CASE rather than per file -- a file that is 4,210 named-character-reference cases is not one answer. It is the only oracle here whose expected output comes from neither this library nor a second implementation: it is the specification's own tests, the ones every browser is checked against. Every runnable case passes, and the floors say so.
//tokens-skipped: 288 cases name an initial state this tokenizer does not have -- PLAINTEXT, which never ends, and the CDATA section state, which the tree builder enters from foreign content. Neither is a state a MARKUP tokenizer needs. They are reported as skipped rather than passed, so a skip can never be mistaken for a pass; the oracle prints the count on every run.
//tokens-why: It closes the one hole nothing else here could reach. The 2,231 named character references are GENERATED from entities.json by a script, and before this suite arrived not a single one of them was checked. namedEntities.test checks all of them, in both spellings.
//lower: The authored Shrubbery HTML corpus lowers with no diagnostic at all. This one is expected to stay at 100%: it is the syntax's own examples.
//survive: Nothing crashes, on anything, and nothing may drop below 100%. `notation` is the 696-file shrubbery corpus and `css` the 350-file CSS corpus, both already in the repository for other suites -- almost none of either is markup, so they are a free adversarial corpus for the parser AND for the lowering, which is pointed at the same bytes.
